genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the man described builds pipe instruments
he selects seasoned wood free of flaws
he melts a metal mixture into thin sheets
these sheets are rolled to form the pipes
the pressure of the bellows must be adjusted
excessive pressure gives a harsh sound
too little pressure weakens the sound
tuning slightly alters the length of the pipes
he stops labouring when his hearing tires
text: The organ builder works slowly, and every movement he makes is a measurement. Wood comes first. He picks out seasoned boards with no knots in them and planes each one until the thickness runs even. Metal comes second. He melts tin and lead together, pours the alloy out in thin sheets, then rolls every sheet into a pipe that trembles the moment air passes through. Air comes last. He sets the pressure of the bellows, for too strong a wind turns the note shrill, while too weak a wind smothers it. Then comes the tuning, the most delicate stage of the lot. The craftsman shortens or lengthens each pipe by a hair's breadth, until the high timbre stops beating against the low one. His ear, he admits, tires long before his hands do, and that is the point at which he lays the work aside.

units: the evening opened with a short piece for the low strings
the opening sound filled the space without excess
a solo singer then performed a work with restraint
the writer stresses how young this performer is
the second half of the programme convinced less
the brass instruments covered the woodwind instruments
an untuned string instrument produced an unpleasant noise
the conductor flagged the mishap with a single glance
the closing chord hung under the ceiling of the hall
the writer judges this ensemble uneven against its ambitions
text: The evening opened with a short piece given to the low strings alone, and their thick sound filled the hall without ever swamping it. A work for solo voice came next, in which the singer shaped every phrase with a restraint one rarely meets in so young a performer. The second half disappointed. The brass, set too far forward, buried the woodwind, and the ear lost the middle line. One badly adjusted string instrument let out a brief grating noise, which the conductor put right with a glance. The closing bars drew every desk together at last, and the final chord hung under the vaulted roof for a stretch that seemed suspended. You came away with the impression of an uneven ensemble, at its finest the moment it gives up on effect, and brittle the moment it reaches for sheer force.

units: the writer is writing from a rehearsal room
the room is unheated and the air inside is damp
the damp warps the wood and slackens the strings
the instrument loses its tuning after half an hour
the retuning eats up half of the session
the person in charge found the same trouble on his bow
his request for a heater was turned down
the group falls back on a narrower room next door
the bare walls of that room amplify the low sounds
the writer asks her correspondent to bring a tuning fork
text: I am writing from the room where we rehearse, having turned up well ahead of anyone else. There is no heating in here, and the damp works straight into my instrument: the wood tightens, the strings go slack, and half an hour later the tuning has gone. Since I have to keep putting it right, I lose half the session, which wears the rest of the group down as well. The one in charge worked out the cause at last, his own bow having started to grate in just the same way. He asked for a heater and was turned down. So we fall back on the room next door, narrower than this one, where the bare walls throw the sound about and set the low notes booming. I would sooner have that fault than the cold. If you come by at the weekend, bring your tuning fork: mine has rung false since I dropped it.

units: a sound professional is asked about her hearing health
she blames the wear on quiet and lengthy mixing sessions
listening at low volume forces sustained attention
she gave up the ear protection she had bought
that protection distorted her sense of the high frequencies
she breaks off her listening at regular intervals
she holds herself to a volume ceiling she never crosses
she sometimes turns down a session when she feels worn out
the evening ringing in her ears has clearly eased
text: What wears out a sound engineer's hearing fastest? She answers without hesitating: not the concerts, but the long mixing sessions at low volume, where the ear strains after details barely there at all. And the remedy? She bought earplugs at first, she says, then let them go, since they muffle the top of the range and throw her judgement out. What works for her comes down to three settled habits. The first is to kill the sound at regular intervals and let the ear rest for a while. The second is a ceiling of loudness she never goes above, however hard the client happens to push. The third, and by far the hardest of them, is to turn a session down flat once she feels her hearing has gone. Since then, she tells us, the ringing that used to buzz around her head at night has all but stopped.

units: two professionals judge the same venue differently
the man finds the sound of the stage too dull
he blames the drapes for soaking up the high frequencies
the singer feels held up there by her voice coming back
the side walls send her own singing back to her
both note that the floor shakes with the low sounds
that shaking upsets the technician's readings
it gives the singer a rhythmic marker
she sings under her breath in the other venue to steady herself
the technician prefers a venue that adds no colour
text: The engineer and the singer do not describe the same hall. He finds the stage dull, blaming the heavy drapes, which soak up the top of the range and hand him back something soft and shapeless. She says the opposite, that the place holds her up, since her own voice comes back to her off the side walls. On one point they agree: the floor shakes as soon as the low notes rise. He treats that as a fault, the trembling muddling every reading he takes. She treats it as a prop, since she feels the beat coming up through her feet before it ever reaches her ear. Asked about the larger hall next door, she owns up to humming under her breath there to steady herself, so hollow does the silence seem. He much prefers it, saying that a space which adds nothing at last lets you hear what is played.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the writer traces early music to three movements of the hand
the first movement consists in striking
a skin stretched over a hollow shell gives a deep carrying sound
the second movement rests on breathing
a hollow pierced plant stem turns breath into a note
stopping or opening the holes varies the pitch
the third movement is that of plucking
a taut string let go gives a short-lived sound
a hollow chamber was added to lengthen the shaking
these three origins can still be read in the shape of the instruments
text: All early music comes down to three movements that the hands learned apart from one another. The first is the blow. A skin stretched over a hollow shell answers the shock and sets the air shivering around it; from there come the drums, whose rumble carries further than any voice. The second rests on breathing. A hollow stem, pierced with holes of unequal size, turns the outgoing breath into a note, and the hand that stops or frees those openings drives the pitch up or down. The third is the pluck. A string held taut between two fixed points gives a short sound when it is drawn back and released; beneath it a hollow chamber was soon added, so that the shaking might last longer and swell. The three families mingled afterwards, yet their origin is still legible in the shape of the instruments.

units: a string that is pulled swings about its resting position
that swinging squeezes then loosens the neighbouring air
the disturbance travels on from one part to the next
the air particles themselves barely move
the outer ear guides the wave towards a passage
a thin membrane begins to swing at the end of that passage
three small bones strengthen that movement
a coiled organ filled with fluid then takes in the shaking
cells fringed with hairs turn the movement into nerve signals
the rate of the swings settles the pitch that is heard
text: A plucked string swings away from where it rested, comes back, then overshoots again, and that coming and going is what we call vibration. It squeezes the air molecules alongside it, which crowd together, loosen, and pass the shove on to the next ones. The disturbance travels outwards from one part to the next, while the air itself covers almost no ground at all. Reaching the outer ear, it is funnelled into a narrow passage, at the far end of which a soft membrane begins to swing at the very same rate. Three minute bones gather that movement, strengthen it, and hand it on to a coiled organ filled with fluid. Inside, cells fringed with hairs bend over and give off an electrical signal. The nerve carries it to the brain, which reads the note as high or low from the rate of the swings.

units: a flaw in the casting had cracked a bell
the crack could not be seen without examination
it split the shaking into two parts out of tune with each other
the ringing gave a beating instead of a clean sound
those living nearby complained without grasping where the noise came from
the local assembly had the bell taken down
a specialist declared the repair impossible
she explained that welding alters the density of the metal
the bell was cast afresh from its own alloy
putting it back in service stopped passers-by where they stood
text: A flaw in the casting, which no eye could catch, had cracked the tower bell. The split ran under the lip of the bronze, and it broke the shaking into two parts that no longer agreed. Every peal therefore gave a dull beating in place of the full sound people expected, and those living nearby, with no notion of the cause, complained of a ringing that seemed to grate. The council had the thing brought down, a slow and costly job. A founder was called in. A crack, she explained, cannot be mended, for welded metal no longer holds the same density, and the timbre suffers by it. She offered instead to melt the whole down and cast it afresh from its own bronze. The recast bell went up as the cold season ended, and its first peal rang so cleanly that passers-by halted in the middle of the square.

units: the text speaks to whoever plays in an overly reverberant room
the notes pile up and blur the fast passages
the rigid walls send the sound back without soaking it up
a clap of the hands serves to gauge how long the tail runs
a rug on the floor treats the bounce between floor and ceiling
a thick fabric is hung on one wall only
covering every wall would leave the room lifeless
moving the stand round to an angle avoids building up the low sounds
a second clap allows the result to be checked
text: You rehearse in a room where every note drags on behind the next, and the quick passages turn to mush. Hard surfaces are the trouble: they send the sound back instead of soaking it up. Work through it by stages. Clap your hands once in the middle of the floor and listen to the tail; the longer it runs, the heavier the treatment will have to be. Lay a thick rug down on the floor next, since the bounce between floor and ceiling is by far the most stubborn of the lot. Hang a heavy blanket on the wall facing your instrument, never on all four, or the room goes lifeless and the top of the range is smothered. Swing the stand round to an angle last of all, because a symmetrical placing builds the low notes up and sets them droning. Clap again: if the tail has halved, leave it there.

units: a student survey compares two neighbouring urban areas
the workshop area suffers a steady mechanical noise
that constant noise ends up slipping past the attention of the neighbours
the area of the main roads shows a lower average level
sudden traffic sounds arise there without warning
it is those sudden peaks that break into rest
one resident sets the steady drone against the harsh sound
the survey also covered the night hours
night deliveries bring on ringing in the ears and tiredness
the authors conclude that the unexpected tires more than the loudness
text: Two neighbouring districts live with noise in opposite ways, and a survey run by students has just borne it out. Over on the workshop side the machines never stop, yet their drone holds steady, and the people living there say they grow so used to it that they stop hearing it. Along the main roads the average level is lower; the trouble is the horns and the squealing brakes, which come out of nowhere, and it is these brief peaks that wake you. One resident puts it plainly: a steady drone you end up forgetting, a sound that stings you never do. The students looked at the nights as well. Where the activity stops, sleep repairs itself; where the deliveries carry on, people complain of ringing in the ears and of tiredness. Their conclusion fits in a line: loudness is not what drains you, surprise is.
